Dinner at my grandparents' flat got loud fast. Saurabh mama slapped the table and said the election result would wreck everything, and my cousin shouted back. Normally I'd have joined one side. That night I kept quiet and thought: he isn't angry about a party, he's angry about something. Slogans are just where it comes out.

So when there was a gap, I asked, "Mama, what are you actually afraid of?" He was quiet, then said, "That the shop will go under, and that you kids won't be safe. I've seen bad years." I realised I wanted the same things: safe family, steady work. We disagreed on how, but under the shouting there was something we shared. Suraj

qa.q: What did Saurabh mama say he was afraid of?
qa.a: That the shop will go under and that the kids won't be safe.

qa.q: What was Saurabh mama really feeling under the shouting, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Saurabh mama was afraid for the shop and the family's safety, which the quiet pause and the words "I've seen bad years" reveal.

qa.q: What could Suraj try next in a conversation with Saurabh mama, and why?
qa.a: Suraj could ask which of those worries feels most pressing and what he has seen in the bad years, because listening to the concern builds trust for a later talk about solutions.

qa.q: How might the cousin who shouted back feel when Suraj asks this question?
qa.a: The cousin may feel surprised that the argument paused, and may see that the shouting had been about worry rather than winning.

grounding: In a heated dinner debate, the student asks what the uncle actually fears and sees that a shared value lies beneath the position.

A note to myself, Sunday night. Gurleen.
I'm writing this down because I want to remember how Salma handled it.
At dinner tonight my husband, her Mamu, got loud about the election again. The candidate from our area, the broken roads, 'things aren't safe any more'. Salma is twenty and studies political science, and I could see her getting ready to argue with the slogans.
Instead she put her spoon down and asked him, 'Mamu, what are you actually worried about?' He started the same speech. She asked again, gently. 'For us, I mean. What scares you?'
He went quiet. Then he said the girls come home late from college, the lane is dark, and last year someone's chain was snatched near the temple. 'I just want the house safe.'
Salma said, 'I want that too. We just disagree about who will do it.' The shouting stopped. They talked for another hour, mostly about streetlights.
I have never seen him listen to her like that.

qa.q: What happened near the temple last year?
How did Mamu feel beneath the loud talk about the election?
qa.a: Worried and protective, afraid for the family's safety, especially the girls coming home late.

qa.q: What else could Salma do in future political arguments at home?
qa.a: Keep asking what worry sits under the slogans, and look for shared goals, like the streetlights, before the disagreements.

qa.q: How does the dinner look to Gurleen, who wrote the note?
qa.a: Gurleen is struck to see her husband really listen to Salma, and wants to remember how one question changed the evening.

grounding: Shows a student in a heated election debate asking what her uncle actually fears and finding a shared concern for family safety.

Diwali night, 11:45. Urmila's diary.
It happened again at dinner. Kiran mama started on the elections the moment the sweets came out, loud, jabbing the table, saying the other side would 'ruin everything we've built'. Last year I would have thrown numbers at him and we'd both have left angry.
This year I tried something Professor Mehta said in class: find the value under the position. So I asked, 'Mama, what do you think we'd lose?'
He looked surprised. He talked about his shop, about the loan he took to expand it, about how scared he is that if prices rise again he won't manage the loan and keep Chintu in college. 'I've worked thirty years for this,' he said, much more quietly.
And I understood. It isn't really about the party. It's about Chintu's fees and thirty years of work.
We still disagree about who should win. But I told him I understood the fear, and he patted my head. First Diwali without a fight.

qa.q: What did Kiran mama take a loan for?
What was Kiran mama afraid of beneath the political talk?
qa.a: He was scared of losing what he had built, of not managing the shop loan and Chintu's college if prices rose again.

qa.q: What could Urmila do if the argument returns next year?
qa.a: Ask the same kind of question, share a view calmly, and acknowledge the fear even while disagreeing about the election.

qa.q: What would change if Urmila had thrown numbers at him as last year?
qa.a: They would likely have argued and left angry again, and the fear about the shop and Chintu's fees would never have come out.

grounding: Shows a student in a heated election argument asking what an uncle fears and finding the worry beneath the slogans.
